## Environmental Education: The Wetland as a Living Classroom

The morning starts early at Charca de Suárez when the school bus parks next to the Interpretation Center. The children get off with binoculars hanging around their necks and field notebooks under their arms, a ritual that is repeated more than five thousand times a year according to the records of the wetland's management team. The figure is not insignificant: in a region where the coastline has suffered intense urban pressure, the fact that thousands of schoolchildren visit this enclave every school year represents a form of symbolic reparation. Nature, so often pushed aside, once again occupies a central place in the education of new generations.

The educational program of the Charca is structured around three complementary axes. Bird identification workshops allow students to recognize the most representative species of the wetland, from the purple swamphen to the purple heron, with the help of specialized guides and optical equipment adapted to their ages. Scientific bird-ringing activities, coordinated by experienced ornithologists, bring students closer to a real research methodology used to study bird migrations and survival. Litter cleanup days complete the cycle with a practical dimension that connects learning with direct care for the environment.

The Motril Department of Education has found in this space a first-rate pedagogical ally. Together with the wetland team, teaching units have been designed that integrate local biodiversity into the school curriculum, so that the visit is not an isolated parenthesis but an extension of what is worked on in the classroom. An elementary school teacher can explain aquatic ecosystems using the concrete example of the Charca, or address the food chain based on the species that the students themselves have observed during the excursion. The abstraction of the textbook is transformed into direct experience.

Scientific bird-ringing deserves special attention for what it represents in terms of environmental literacy. Schoolchildren witness the complete process: capture with mist nets, taking biometric measurements, placing the metal ring, and releasing the bird. This is not a spectacle, but a rigorous practice that introduces children to the scientific method without artifice. The expression of amazement when a common reed warbler perches for a few seconds in the ringer's hand before flying away is, according to the center's educators, one of the most effective moments for sowing a consciousness of respect toward wildlife.

The cleanup days add a layer of civic responsibility that transcends the purely biological. Students walk the trails and perimeter areas of the wetland collecting waste that, for the most part, is carried by runoff from the urban and agricultural environment. The activity is accompanied by a guided reflection on the origin of those wastes and their impact on aquatic ecosystems. The message sinks in more powerfully when it is formulated on the ground, with full bags and muddy hands, than from the blackboard of a conventional classroom.

The Interpretation Center functions as both the gateway and the preparatory workspace before heading out to the trails. Its explanatory panels, wetland models, and audiovisual resources allow visitors to contextualize what will later be observed in the field. Educators use these facilities to introduce basic concepts about Mediterranean wetlands, their fragility, and their importance as biodiversity refuges on a densely humanized coastline. The visit is structured in two parts: first the theory at the center, then the practice at the observation points and boardwalks.

Collaboration between the local administration and the management team has allowed the educational offering to be maintained throughout the entire school year, with seasonal adaptations that take advantage of changes in the bird community. In winter, schoolchildren can observe the wintering waterfowl arriving from northern Europe; in spring, they witness the spectacle of breeding and the arrival of summer species. This variability makes the wetland a renewable educational resource, different on each visit, that invites return visits.

The stated goal of the program is to foster a culture of environmental respect from childhood, a goal pursued without grandiloquent speeches. Educators insist that the aim is not to train future ornithologists, but to create an emotional bond with the territory that endures into adult life. A child who has seen a kingfisher dive into the water surface will hardly forget that image, and that memory operates as an emotional anchor when, years later, they must make decisions as a citizen or as a consumer.

Participation data confirm the consolidation of the project. More than five thousand schoolchildren per year from educational centers in Motril and other municipalities of the Granada coast pass through Charca de Suárez, a figure that far exceeds that of many protected natural areas with greater extension and budget. The proximity to the urban center, just a few minutes by bus, reduces travel costs and facilitates the inclusion of the visit within school hours without the need for major logistics.

The educational program of the Charca is not limited to elementary school students. Secondary schools in the region also participate with activities adapted to biology and geology content, while vocational training programs related to environmental management use the wetland as a practice laboratory. This educational continuity extends the scope of the project and integrates it into a more ambitious educational strategy that accompanies students from childhood to youth.

Teacher involvement is decisive for the success of the initiative. Participating teachers receive preparatory materials and guidelines to prepare the visit in class, so that the outing is not perceived as an extracurricular activity disconnected from the curriculum. The teaching units developed jointly by the department and the wetland team include evaluation proposals and extension activities that allow the work to continue once the excursion is finished. The wetland thus becomes a living classroom integrated into the regular programming.

The social dimension of the educational program also deserves careful consideration. In a city like Motril, where intensive agriculture and the service sector shape the economic structure, the Charca offers schoolchildren direct contact with a natural heritage that many did not know despite living a short distance away. Surveys conducted among participating students reveal that a significant proportion visit the wetland for the first time through the school program, a fact that underscores the compensatory function of this initiative.

The wetland team has managed to adapt the discourse to different educational levels without losing scientific rigor. With the youngest, they work through play and sensory exploration; with the older ones, through analysis of real data and discussion of concrete environmental problems. This methodological flexibility, combined with the quality of the environment, explains why the demand for school visits grows year after year and why many centers repeat the experience annually. Charca de Suárez has become, without explicitly intending to, the best ambassador for its own conservation.
